title: Family emergency plan and meeting points
def: A family emergency plan says how you will reach each other, where you will meet near home and out of the neighborhood, and who an out-of-area contact is.
look: a meeting spot near home and one farther away
an out-of-area contact everyone knows
phone numbers written on paper
use: Write the plan down, give every family member a card, and practice it twice a year.
not: Do not rely only on phones; networks fail in disasters.

title: What to teach a child about being lost in the woods
def: A child who is lost should stay in one place, hug a tree, make noise, and answer when called; searchers find children who stay put far faster.
look: a whistle on the child's jacket
bright clothing
the child knows nobody will be angry
use: Teach: stop, hug a tree, blow the whistle three times, stay put, and answer anyone calling your name. Practice it as a game.
not: Do not teach a child to keep walking to find the way, and do not scold them when found.
call: If a child is missing outdoors, call 911 right away; do not wait.

title: How a child calls 911
def: Children can call 911 from any phone, even a locked one, and should say what happened, where they are, and stay on the line.
look: how to reach emergency call on your phone's lock screen
the child knows their address
a calm practice run with a turned-off phone
use: Teach your address, how to place an emergency call on a locked phone, and to answer the dispatcher's questions and stay on the line.
not: Do not let children practice on a live line, and do not teach them to hang up if they make a mistake; they should stay and explain.

title: Keeping children warm and spotting cold stress in infants
def: Children lose heat faster than adults; an infant with hypothermia can have bright red, cold skin and very low energy.
look: bright red, cold skin in a baby
a quiet, floppy, or very sleepy child
shivering, clumsy hands, or slurred speech in an older child
use: Dress children in one more layer than adults, cover the head, change wet clothes at once, and warm a cold child against your body in a dry blanket.
not: Do not use hot water bottles or heaters directly on a child's skin.
call: Call 911 for an infant with cold, red skin and low energy, or any child who is confused or unresponsive.

title: Dehydration and fever in a child
also: when to take child to doctor
def: Children dehydrate quickly with vomiting, diarrhea, heat, or fever; a dry mouth, few wet diapers, no tears, and unusual sleepiness are warning signs.
look: fewer wet diapers or no urine for many hours
no tears when crying, a dry mouth, sunken eyes
fever with a stiff neck, rash, or trouble breathing
use: Give small, frequent sips of fluid or oral rehydration solution, keep the child cool, and watch urine and alertness.
not: Do not give aspirin to children, and do not give plain water alone to an infant under six months for dehydration; ask a clinician.
call: Call a doctor for an infant under 3 months with any fever. Call 911 for a child who is very sleepy, hard to wake, or breathing hard.

title: Kids outdoors: ticks, poison ivy, water, and firearms
def: A few short rules prevent most outdoor harm to children: check for ticks, avoid leaves of three, stay within reach near water, and never touch a gun.
look: a tick check after every outing
a life jacket on near water
guns stored locked and unloaded
use: Teach: if you see a gun, don't touch, leave, tell an adult. Keep children within arm's reach near water and do a full tick check at night.
not: Do not leave children alone near water, even for a moment, or store firearms where a child can reach them.

title: Infant formula when the water is unsafe
def: When tap water is unsafe, infant formula should be ready-to-feed, or mixed with bottled water or water that was boiled and cooled.
look: a boil-water notice
flooding near the well
no power to boil water
use: Use ready-to-feed formula when you can; otherwise use bottled water or water brought to a rolling boil for one minute and cooled. Clean bottles in safe water.
not: Do not use water from a flooded well or treated only with a filter for an infant without checking with your health department.

title: A child left in a vehicle is an emergency
def: A closed car heats up fast even on a mild day and can kill a child within minutes; in winter, a running car can fill with exhaust.
look: a child alone in a car
a sweaty, red, or unresponsive child
a running car with snow blocking the tailpipe
use: If you see a child alone in a hot car, call 911 at once and follow the dispatcher's directions. Make a habit of checking the back seat every time you leave the car.
not: Do not leave a child in a car for any time, even with the windows cracked or the engine running.

title: Pet kit, pet evacuation, and pet poisoning
def: Pets need their own emergency kit and a plan for where they can stay, because many shelters only take service animals.
look: food, water, medicines, leash, carrier, and records
a list of pet-friendly hotels or friends
an ID tag and microchip
use: Pack a pet kit, plan pet-friendly places to stay, and take pets with you if you evacuate.
not: Do not guess about a pet poisoning; call your veterinarian or an animal poison line.
call: Call your veterinarian or an animal poison control line for any suspected pet poisoning.
